tier_reason: First-party BenchmarkDotNet table in the README against a scalar System.Math.Exp/Log loop; benchmark code is public (LitMathBenchmarks/ExpBenchmark.cs, LogBenchmark.cs) but no CPU model and no .NET runtime version are given for the current table, and the committed ExpBenchmark uses Params(3_200_000), not the N=64/100000 shown, so the run configuration is not in public sources.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Current README (AVX-512 section, .NET 8): Exp N=100000 NaiveExpDouble 354,491.80 ns vs LitExpDouble 64,727.96 ns (5.5x, derived from page data); Log N=100000 259,985.93 ns vs 35,793.39 ns (7.3x, derived from page data; README text says 7.5x); N=64 Exp 218.69 ns vs 42.34 ns (5.2x, derived), Log 137.06 ns vs 24.89 ns (5.5x, derived). An earlier README table (commit 3d4c302, Nov 2023, AVX2 era, removed on 2023-11-16) shows LitExpDouble vs naive 1.7x at N=3, 3.3x at N=64, 3.1x at N=2048, 2.8x at N=65536 and 2.4x at N=32,000,000, and vs MKL.NET Vml.Exp: LitMath faster at N=3 (6.675 vs 29.871 ns, 4.5x), N=64 (71.946 vs 116.934 ns, 1.6x) and N=2048 (2,446 vs 3,239 ns, 1.3x), but MKL faster at N=65536 (19,160 vs 82,346 ns, 4.3x) and N=32,000,000 (23.7 ms vs 47.1 ms, 2.0x) (ratios derived from page data). The README's '10x versus MKL' remark is not backed by any table.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.1 (LitMathBenchmarks.csproj targets net6.0 and net8.0); the runtime used for the README table is not stated; AVX-512 paths need .NET 8
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the current table (an AVX-512 machine; the author's Zen 3 dev machine has no AVX-512). The MKL comparison was on an unnamed Zen 3 CPU.
corrections.caveats: No CPU model or runtime version beside the table; the README calls the AVX-512 numbers preliminary. The committed ExpBenchmark.cs (last changed Dec 2022) runs N=3,200,000 only, so the published Exp N=64/100000 rows came from an uncommitted configuration. Benchmark inputs are built with C# integer division: LogBenchmark at N=64 computes Log(1.0) for all 64 elements (degenerate input), and ExpBenchmark feeds Log(k) for integers k=0..100 (about 1% -Infinity at N=100000), so inputs cover a narrow range. The naive loops store into a single scalar field while LitMath writes an output array. MKL.NET Vml.Exp beats LitMath at N=65536 and above in the author's own older table; the '10x vs MKL' claim has no table. ATan accuracy is 1e-10 versus 1e-15 for Sin, Log and Cos. C#/.NET library, not C++.
corrections.baseline: naive scalar loop over System.Math.Exp and System.Math.Log (NaiveExpDouble, NaiveLogDouble); an older README table also compared Intel MKL via MKL.NET Vml.Exp

notes: Numbers match the README; ratios are 5.2-7.3x versus a scalar .NET Math loop with AVX-512, about 2.4-3.3x in the older AVX2 table. Shortcomings to record: no CPU model or runtime version, published Exp configuration not in the repo, degenerate integer-division inputs (Log N=64 is all 1.0), MKL faster at large N in the author's own older table, stale since 2024-03-28, C# rather than C++.

tier_reason: First-party README states one ratio (about 2.3x versus np.amin followed by np.amax) with no published table, no CPU model and no compiler stated for the run; the benchmark script scripts/perf_benchmark.py is public but its output is not published.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Measurement compiler not stated; the build file numpy_minmax/_minmax_cffi.py sets -O3 -Wall (-Wextra on POSIX) -mavx -mavx512f on x86, and CHANGELOG 0.2.1 says Linux wheels are built with clang. Benchmark: scripts/perf_benchmark.py (time.time, numpy pair timed once, minmax median of 5, diplib also compared).
corrections.caveats: One headline ratio, no table, no CPU model ('Intel CPU'), measured against numpy 1.24-1.26 while the package has required numpy>=2,<3 since 0.4.0 (2025-03), so the claim predates the current baseline. scripts/perf_benchmark.py times np.amin+np.amax once but takes the median of 5 minmax runs, and prints times without published output; the win on large arrays is expected from one pass versus two over memory. Semantics differ from NumPy: NaN is not propagated (minps/maxps and < comparisons drop NaN; np.amin/np.amax return NaN) and the tests have no NaN case. Only float32 (C/F-contiguous or 1-D strided) and contiguous int16 are accelerated; other inputs fall back to np.amin/np.amax. The int16 AVX2 path runs without a CPUID check and the whole C file is compiled with -mavx512f. ARM has no NEON path.
corrections.workload: Minimum and maximum of float32 NumPy arrays (C/F-contiguous or 1-D strided; up to 999,999,999 elements in the script, plus 100,000 small 9-element and 3x9 arrays) and contiguous int16 arrays in one pass using AVX/AVX-512 (C via cffi).

notes: Ratio matches the README text; no table exists. Shortcomings to record: single unsourced ratio with no CPU model, measured on numpy 1.x while the current release targets numpy 2.x, asymmetric timing (one numpy run versus median of 5), NaN not propagated unlike NumPy, AVX2 int16 path without a CPU check. Last code change 2026-02-06 (Python 3.14); last commit 2026-06-04 is a dependency bump; PyPI 0.6.0.

tier_reason: First-party criterion tables in the README with CPU models; benchmark code is public (bench/alts.rs now, bench/compete.rs when the adler rows were measured) and the opt-level comes from Cargo.toml, but the rustc version is never stated, so not A.

corrections.baseline: adler/adler2 crates (scalar Rust Adler-32; adler2 is the maintained successor used by miniz_oxide) and adler32 crate, plus wuffs std/adler32 built with gcc
corrections.claimed_speedup: README, i5-8300H Windows 10: 10k simd-adler32 212.61 ns (43.805 GiB/s) vs adler32 4.8084 us (1.9369 GiB/s, 22.6x derived from page data) vs adler 17.979 us (530.43 MiB/s, 84.6x derived) vs wuffs 3843 ns (2.63 GiB/s, 16.7x derived); 100k 33.320 GiB/s vs adler32 1.9207 GiB/s (17.3x derived). i9-9880H macOS 10k: 46.480 GiB/s vs adler32 2.2433 GiB/s (20.7x derived). Apple M3 Pro 10k: 37.090 GiB/s vs adler32 3.3894 GiB/s (10.9x derived) vs adler2 6.1280 GiB/s (6.1x derived).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: criterion 0.3 benches (bench/alts.rs; the older bench/compete.rs produced the adler rows); Cargo.toml [profile.release] opt-level = 2, debug = true, inherited by cargo bench; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated (runtime CPU feature detection, so no target-cpu needed); wuffs row ran as 'wuffs bench -ccompilers=gcc -reps=1 -iterscale=300 std/adler32' under mingw64
corrections.stars_or_usage: 49 stars; crates.io simd-adler32 439,768,193 downloads (161,755,577 recent) as of 2026-10-11
corrections.caveats: rustc version not stated. The 85x figure is against the old adler 1.0.2 crate at opt-level 2, which ran slower than adler32 in the same table; the fairer incumbent ratios are about 17-23x versus adler32 on x86 and about 6x versus adler2 on Apple M3 Pro (derived from page data). The wuffs row ran through a different harness (gcc under mingw64). The macOS 100k/adler row is internally inconsistent: 83.776 us for 100,000 bytes is about 1138 MiB/s, but the table prints 534.69 MiB/s (copied from the Windows table). The x86 tables predate the May 2026 switch of the benches from adler to adler2. Heavy use of unsafe SIMD code, fuzzed with afl before release. Arguably a checksum library rather than a general SIMD intrinsics library.

notes: All quoted numbers are on the README; criterion harness is symmetric (same random buffer, result black-boxed). Shortcomings to record: no rustc version, 85x ratio is against a slow old adler crate (6x versus adler2 on M3 Pro is the fair incumbent figure), one copy error in the macOS 100k/adler throughput, wuffs row from a different harness. Very widely used despite 49 stars (about 440M crates.io downloads).
